### Communicating Across Levels

Data-aware design breaks top-down, "gut"-based decision-making. Data collected via A/B testing, ethnographic field research, field deployments, surveys, lab studies, and usability research grounds decisions and reduces risk compared to relying on executive hunches. A 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield titled "Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO" addressed this. Data resolves conflicts without relying on rank or politics.

John Ciancutti (former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix) described how data literacy across roles at Netflix became a source of freedom and innovation. Patty McCord (former Chief Talent Officer at Netflix for over 12 years) noted that having a mechanism to measure whether you are doing right by customers allows more people to have a voice in product development.

At Netflix, the data-driven approach was well established and universally accepted, starting from CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt but embraced by all levels. McCord said: "At Netflix, the CEO doesn't get to do whatever he wants." Any employee, including executives, can get caught up thinking they know the answer. A/B testing mitigates top-down problem solving because everyone can learn from experimentation. When Reed Hastings had a strong product idea, he submitted it to the same A/B testing rigor as everyone else. On rare occasions he might dictate the exact way an idea would work, but only on "his test cell" — that cell was tested against others proposed by the product team. If it didn't win, it didn't launch. Upper management holding themselves accountable to the same process reinforced subjecting ideas to grounded review and the possibility of "failing" as a positive outcome. This value was central to a view of how the company should work.

To shift into a data-aware framework, examine how product and design decisions have been made. If decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, ensure those people recognize the value of bringing in user data, as their individual weight (and your own) will be diminished. Check yourself: are you comfortable seeing how incorporating data changes the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process?

## Statistical Methods Used in Our Research

This appendix describes the statistical techniques used in the research presented in *Accelerate*.

**Survey Design and Data Collection.** The research relied on surveys to collect data. The authors used established psychometric principles to design the survey instrument, ensuring questions were clear, unambiguous, and measured the intended constructs. They collected data from a large, diverse sample of technology professionals across multiple organizations.

**Factor Analysis.** To validate that survey questions grouped together as expected (e.g., questions about deployment frequency, lead time, and mean time to recover forming a single "software delivery performance" factor), the authors used **confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)**. CFA tests whether the data fit a hypothesized measurement model. They also used **exploratory factor analysis (EFA)** in earlier stages to identify underlying structures without pre-specified groupings.

**Reliability and Validity.** The authors assessed **internal consistency reliability** using Cronbach's alpha (target ≥ 0.70) and composite reliability. They evaluated **convergent validity** (items measuring the same construct correlate highly) and **discriminant validity** (items measuring different constructs do not correlate too highly). For discriminant validity, they used the Fornell-Larcker criterion and examined cross-loadings.

**Structural Equation Modeling (SEM).** The primary analytical method was **partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM)**. PLS-SEM is well-suited for exploratory research and complex models with many constructs, indicators, and paths. It does not require normally distributed data and works with smaller sample sizes than covariance-based SEM. The authors used PLS-SEM to test the hypothesized relationships between capabilities (e.g., continuous delivery, lean management) and outcomes (e.g., software delivery performance, organizational performance).

**Path Coefficients and Significance.** Path coefficients (β) represent the strength and direction of relationships between constructs. Statistical significance was assessed using **bootstrapping** (a resampling technique) to generate t-statistics and p-values. The authors report standard errors and confidence intervals for path coefficients.

**Effect Sizes.** Beyond significance, the authors report **effect sizes (f²)** to indicate the practical importance of a predictor. Cohen's guidelines classify f² values of 0.02, 0.15, and 0.35 as small, medium, and large effects, respectively.

**Common Method Bias.** Because all data came from a single survey at one point in time, the authors tested for **common method bias** using Harman's single-factor test and a marker variable approach. Results indicated that common method bias was not a significant concern.

**Control Variables.** The models included control variables such as organization size, industry, and years of experience to rule out alternative explanations for the findings.

**Limitations.** The authors acknowledge that the research is **cross-sectional** (data collected at one point in time), so causal claims are limited. They also note that the sample is self-selected and may not be fully representative of all technology organizations. Future research should use longitudinal designs and objective performance data where possible.
